title: AscendGYM: A Cost-Aware Kernel Optimization Benchmark for Real-World Workloads on Ascend NPUs
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 13 Nov 2026]
Title:AscendGYM: A Cost-Aware Kernel Optimization Benchmark for Real-World Workloads on Ascend NPUs
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Kernel optimization is essential for efficient large language model (LLM) training and inference on Ascend NPUs. Existing Ascend kernel benchmarks primarily focus on kernel generation, with less emphasis on the ability of agents to optimize existing implementations under input configurations drawn from real workloads. To address this requirement, we introduce AscendGYM, a benchmark whose initial suite comprises 48 kernels across three difficulty levels. Each kernel is paired with test cases whose data types and tensor shapes are collected from real-world training and inference tasks. Consequently, performance improvements on AscendGYM map directly to the corresponding workloads. In terms of usability, two evaluation modes are supported in AscendGYM: model evaluation and model-harness evaluation. The kernel optimization capabilities of both trained models and custom agents are allowed to be measured. It provides a complete execution environment that closely reproduces how Ascend kernels are invoked in practical pipelines. For model evaluation, it additionally includes a built-in harness equipped with search orchestration and experience accumulation. Finally, we propose a new metric, the Speedup-Token Score (STS), which quantifies performance gains relative to token cost. By jointly considering speedup and cost, STS enables the assessment of practical kernel optimization capability of a model or harness under an acceptable budget. AscendGYM is available at this https URL.

report.summary: AscendGYM benchmarks AI agents and models at optimizing 48 real-workload kernels on Huawei Ascend NPUs, introducing a cost-aware Speedup-Token Score that weighs speed gains against token spend.
report.background: GPU/NPU kernel optimization is the unglamorous work that decides whether large language models train and serve efficiently. For years the tooling and benchmarks around this have been CUDA-centric, but Huawei's Ascend NPUs and its CANN software stack now run a meaningful share of Chinese AI workloads, and their kernel ecosystem is far less mature. Recent research has turned LLM agents loose on writing and tuning GPU kernels, and benchmarks such as KernelBench exist to measure them. Those benchmarks, however, mostly reward generating a kernel from scratch; AscendGYM's authors argue the real job is optimizing existing implementations under the tensor shapes and data types that production training and inference actually produce. Meanwhile, agentic optimization burns tokens, so capability must be judged against cost, not just peak speedup.
key_points: The initial suite has 48 kernels split across three difficulty levels. Crucially, each kernel's test cases use data types and tensor shapes harvested from real training and inference workloads, so speedups measured on AscendGYM are meant to translate directly to the corresponding production pipelines rather than to synthetic shapes.

AscendGYM supports two evaluation modes: model evaluation for trained models, and model-harness evaluation for custom agents. A full execution environment reproduces how Ascend kernels are actually invoked inside practical pipelines, so results reflect deployment-style conditions rather than isolated microbenchmarks.

For model evaluation it ships a built-in harness with search orchestration and experience accumulation, letting an agent iteratively try variants and reuse what it learned. This tests the whole optimization loop—propose, compile, measure, refine—not just one-shot code generation.

The paper proposes the Speedup-Token Score (STS), which quantifies performance gains relative to token cost. By combining speedup and spend, STS measures practical kernel optimization capability under a realistic budget instead of rewarding agents that brute-force search with unlimited tokens.
report.impact: For the AI industry, AscendGYM signals that the non-NVIDIA accelerator stack is getting its own agentic-optimization infrastructure, which matters as Ascend clusters scale. The cost-aware STS metric is arguably the bigger idea: as agent-driven coding matures, benchmarks that ignore token spend will overstate real capability, and STS offers a template other kernel and compiler benchmarks can copy. For developers, it provides a concrete target for building kernel-tuning agents, and the open environment lowers the barrier to experimenting on Ascend without owning a cluster. For regular users, the downstream effect is cheaper, faster LLM inference and training on Ascend hardware—fewer wasted compute cycles, lower serving costs, and less pressure on scarce accelerator capacity.
report.tools: AscendGYM itself is the starting point (code released with the paper). To follow up, look at Huawei's CANN toolkit and Ascend C for writing kernels, and Triton-Ascend for a higher-level path; compare methodologies with KernelBench (CUDA) and Triton's autotuning work. For harness ideas, study agent search frameworks and experience-replay setups, and watch how STS-style cost metrics propagate into other optimization benchmarks.
